headline: High: ECC’s writable, networked, MCP-enabled workspace can conflict with Authelia’s OAuth/ForwardAuth surface, creating default-path data leakage and cascading misconfiguration risk.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ECC reads and writes local files, uses MCP, and treats skills/commands/hooks as workflow surfaces, so attacker-controlled content in shared files or MCP inputs could steer it. Authelia exposes OAuth2/OpenID Connect and ForwardAuth, but no shared channel is documented, so the interaction is inferred rather than proven. Uncertainty keeps this at medium.
conditions: IF ECC ingests Authelia-generated files or MCP payloads as trusted instructions, injection is possible.
IF both agents share a writable workspace or hook directory, malicious content can bridge them.
mitigations: Disable shared writable folders between the two agents.
Require provenance labels on files passed from Authelia to ECC.
Turn off MCP routes that accept untrusted text.
Review and pin ECC hooks/skills before use.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and provenance checks at the orchestrator boundary.

B_data_leakage.rationale: ECC explicitly touches session summaries, agent definitions, git history, documentation, and security findings, and it has broad filesystem read/write plus network egress to external services. Authelia handles authentication flows and broad network egress, so if they share a workspace or credentials, sensitive material can flow into ECC outputs or third-party APIs. The exact shared path is undocumented, so medium is the conservative choice.
conditions: IF Authelia artifacts or secrets are placed in ECC-readable paths, ECC can ingest them.
IF ECC forwards its context to GitHub, Supabase, Vercel, Railway, or Nutrient API, leaked data can leave the boundary.
mitigations: Keep Authelia configs and secrets outside ECC-readable directories.
Restrict ECC network destinations to a test tenant.
Rotate any credentials exposed in shared files.
Audit ECC logs for secret-bearing prompts.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem and egress isolation.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ECC can execute shell, modify git state, write files, and spawn subprocesses; Authelia has broad network egress and OAuth/ForwardAuth integration points. If both operate on the same repo or config tree, concurrent writes and auth-state changes can race and corrupt state. Because ECC’s concurrency model already warns about separate roots, the default overlap is dangerous enough for high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same git repository or config directory, state conflicts can occur.
IF Authelia-managed auth files are edited while ECC runs hooks or skills, writes can race.
mitigations: Use separate roots for each agent immediately.
Pause ECC while Authelia config changes are applied.
Protect shared repos with a lock file or branch policy.
Limit ECC to read-only mode for Authelia-managed paths.
requires-engineering: add transactional locking around shared mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: ECC’s skills and session summaries can turn prior outputs into reusable guidance, while Authelia’s ForwardAuth/OIDC surface can operationalize those outputs in access-control workflows. If ECC consumes Authelia-generated instructions or config suggestions without verification, a mistaken recommendation can cascade into repeated misconfiguration. The pathway exists, but no direct evidence shows automatic action-taking, so medium fits.
conditions: IF ECC stores Authelia-derived guidance in skills or session summaries, errors can persist across sessions.
IF Authelia config changes are applied from ECC output without review, misconfigurations can propagate.
mitigations: Require human review before applying ECC-generated auth changes.
Mark Authelia-derived notes as untrusted in ECC.
Delete stale session summaries after config changes.
Compare ECC suggestions against Authelia docs before execution.
requires-engineering: add verification gates before any auth-related action.

E_compliance.rationale: Authelia is an authentication service with no touched data classes listed, while ECC explicitly handles session summaries, agent definitions, git history, and security findings. The profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch, but ECC’s retention and logging surfaces could still conflict with stricter handling of auth-related records if those records are stored there. Only ECC is cited because the compliance concern is its retention surface.
conditions: IF Authelia authentication logs or user identifiers are stored in ECC session files, retention policy mismatch becomes relevant.
IF ECC retains security findings longer than the operator’s policy allows, compliance exposure increases.
mitigations: Set a short retention window for ECC session files.
Exclude auth logs from ECC storage.
Document which data classes may enter ECC.
Purge old session summaries now.
requires-engineering: align retention and deletion workflows across both systems.
